study.title: Ezekiel 26 - The judgment against Tyre for his pride and joy before the fall of Jerusalem
study.overview: Ezekiel 26 announces God's judgment against Tyre because she rejoiced at the ruin of Jerusalem, as if the fall of the rival city opened the way for her own commercial gains. The chapter develops, in strong and imagery language, the total reversal of Tyre's expectation: what seemed opportunity to become devastation. The text shows God raising up many nations and, more specifically, Nebuchadnezzar as an instrument of judgment. The prophecy ends with the promise of complete desolation, public shame and disappearance of the city as a recognizable center.

outline.title: The joy of Tyre in the face of the fall of Jerusalem and the first judgment of judgment
outline.explanation: The chapter begins by dating the word of the LORD and exposing the sin of Tyre: it mocked the destruction of Jerusalem and imagined commercial profit with the emptiness left by the fallen city. God responds by declaring himself against Tyre and promising the arrival of many nations as waves of the sea. The image highlights that the same coastal city that profited from the sea will be irresistibly attacked and will be reduced to public ruin.

outline.title: Nebuchadnezzar as an agent of siege and material and cultural destruction
outline.explanation: The prophecy now appoints Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, as an instrument of the attack. The siege, the rams, the horses and the bang of the military advance describe the invasion in a concrete way. The text emphasizes that Tyre will lose riches, commodities, houses, walls and also the sound of his songs and harps, indicating not only economic devastation, but the end of his public and celebratory life. The final sentence of the bloc states that it will not be rebuilt as before.

outline.title: The regional impact of the fall and the final sentence of disappearance
outline.explanation: The final verses widen the scene: the princes of the sea, the islands and coastal lands tremble at the fall of Tyre, lamenting their ruined greatness. The city is described as being taken to the abyss, pit and depths of the earth, a language that communicates extreme humiliation and irreversible end. The closure declares that Tyre will be an object of astonishment and will no longer be found.

study.context: The given notes place this prophecy in the same period as the fall of Jerusalem in the eleventh year, although the exact month is not informed in the chapter. Tyndale and Adam Clarke note that Tyre's reaction to the collapse of Jerusalem involved trade interest: Jerusalem was a center of exchange, and its ruin seemed to open new routes and markets to Tyre. The notes also highlight that Tyre was a well-known maritime city linked to international trade, which explains why its fall would produce broad commotion between coastal peoples and sea-linked rulers. Matthew Henry underlines the contrast between Tyre's previous greatness and his later humiliation.
study.theology: The chapter presents God's sovereignty over the nations and about economic and military history. Tyre does not fall by chance, but because the LORD decides to judge her by her pride and for her undue joy before the disgrace of Jerusalem. The language of many nations and Nebuchadnezzar shows that God can use concrete political powers as instruments of his will, without ceasing to be the Lord of action. There is also a theme of moral retribution: whoever rejoices at the fall of the people of God and boasts in advantages obtained through the ruin of others ends up experiencing shame, loss and desolation. Finally, the text reinforces that divine judgment reaches not only military structures, but culture, trade, prestige and public memory.

scholarViews.insight: Shooting rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem because it eliminated a commercial rival and could open new routes and markets for her.
The prophecy is dated in the year in which Jerusalem was taken, and the text exposes the pleasure with which Tyre contemplated the ruins of the city.
Jerusalem is treated as a major center of trade, and Tyre imagines that he will receive for himself the goods that passed through it.

questions: What kind of attitude does the text denounce when a city or person rejoices at the ruin of another to gain self-exence?
How does the description of the siege and fall of Tyre help to understand that God acts in history by concrete means and not just by abstract ideas?
In what areas of today's life - economics, prestige, culture or security - do we need to remember that everything can be shaken by the judgment and sovereignty of God?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to reject the joy for the fall of the other and to examine the heart in the face of gains obtained through the loss of others. It also teaches not to rely on economic power, commercial networks, urban beauty or political influence as if they were permanent. Practical application is to cultivate humility, compassion, and fear of God, recognizing that the Lord can reverse in an instant what the human being judges solid. For the community of faith, the text also invites not to seek revenge or applaud the ruin of adversaries, but to remember that God is the one who judges with righteousness.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow you to safely determine the exact month of verse 1; only the year is highlighted. There are also differences of emphasis between the commentators on the literal extension of the prophecy about the disappearance of Tyre: some treat it as strict historical fulfillment, while others read it as a language that points to the total ruin of the ancient city. The biblical text of the chapter, however, is the main basis of this reading.
